## Adversarial Review Findings — Story 2.3 "Produkt bewerten"

- **AuthorName is never trimmed server-side, so the "resubmission replaces" guarantee (AC 3) only holds for clients that go through the Angular frontend.** `RatingService.SubmitRatingAsync` matches on the raw `authorName` string against `(ProductId, AuthorName)`. The frontend calls `.trim()` before sending (`product-detail.ts:54`), but `SubmitRatingRequest.AuthorName` has only `[Required(AllowEmptyStrings = false)]` (which rejects whitespace-only input but does **not** trim), and the service never normalizes the value before the `Where` filter or the `Add`. A direct API call (curl, Postman, a future mobile client) sending `"Anna "` and `"Anna"` creates two separate rows for what a human would consider the same author — silently violating the one-rating-per-author invariant the whole feature is built on. A business rule this central shouldn't live only in the UI layer.

- **The `catch (DbUpdateException)` fallback in `RatingService.SubmitRatingAsync` is far too broad and can fabricate a "success" response for a rating that was never saved.** It's written to handle exactly one scenario (a concurrent insert for the same `(ProductId, AuthorName)` landing between the `ExecuteUpdateAsync` miss and the `Add`), but `DbUpdateException` also fires for e.g. a value that exceeds the implicit `nvarchar(450)` column width, or a FK violation if the product was deleted in the TOCTOU window between the `AnyAsync` existence check and `SaveChangesAsync`. In both of those real cases, the retried `ExecuteUpdateAsync` matches zero rows (does nothing), and the method falls through to compute and return an aggregate as if the submission succeeded — the controller returns `200 OK` with `Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewertung!` shown on the frontend even though nothing was persisted. A ~450+ character author name is a trivially reachable trigger for this since there's no length validation anywhere in the stack (see next point).

- **No `[StringLength]`/`[MaxLength]` on `AuthorName` anywhere** — not on `SubmitRatingRequest`, not on the `Rating` entity, not in `RatingConfiguration`. The 450-character ceiling that exists today is an accidental byproduct of EF Core's default column size for a string used in a composite primary key; if the schema ever changes (e.g., a surrogate key is introduced), that incidental guard disappears entirely and there is no length bound left at all, silent or otherwise.

- **Zero access control / no protection against author-name impersonation.** Anyone who knows or guesses another visitor's display name can overwrite that person's rating for a product just by POSTing the same `authorName` with a different `score` — the composite PK on `(ProductId, AuthorName)` is the entire "ownership" model. This may be an accepted simplification for a seed project, but it's not called out anywhere in the diff or in `deferred-work.md` as a conscious trade-off, so it reads as an oversight rather than a decision.

- **Aggregate computation (`AverageRating`/`RatingCount` from a full `Select(...).ToListAsync()` over `Score`) is duplicated verbatim between `RatingService.SubmitRatingAsync` and `CatalogService.GetProductDetailAsync`**, with no shared helper. Any future change (e.g., rounding rules, excluding flagged ratings) has two call sites to remember to update, and the diff didn't refactor the existing one when adding the second.

- **Aggregation is done in application memory rather than pushed to the database.** Both call sites pull every `Score` row for the product into a `List<int>` and call `.Average()`/`.Count` in the CLR instead of using EF's `AverageAsync()`/`CountAsync()`. For a seed dataset this is invisible, but it's a pattern now established twice in the codebase, and it's exactly the kind of thing that becomes a real cost once rating volume grows.

- **The riskiest code path in the change — the `DbUpdateException` retry/fallback branch — has zero test coverage.** All four `RatingServiceTests` exercise only the straight-line paths (new rating, same-author replace, different authors, unknown product). Nothing simulates the concurrent-insert race the comment block explicitly describes and defends; the one piece of logic dense enough to need a comment explaining it is also the one piece nobody bothered to test.

- **No test at all for `RatingsController` or for the DTO validation attributes.** `[Required(AllowEmptyStrings = false)]` on `AuthorName` and `[Range(1, 5)]` on `Score` are load-bearing for AC 2 (client validation) but nothing verifies a `Score = 0`, `Score = 6`, or empty-`AuthorName` request actually yields a 400. This extends the project's already-documented "no controller test pattern" gap (called out for `ProductsController` in `deferred-work.md`) rather than closing it, even though this story introduces the project's first mutating endpoint — arguably the endpoint that most needs a request-level test.

- **Frontend collapses all HTTP failure modes into one generic message.** `submitRating()`'s `error` handler in `product-detail.ts:74-77` sets the same `'Bewertung konnte nicht gespeichert werden. Bitte Eingaben prüfen.'` regardless of whether the server returned 400 (bad input — message is appropriate), 404 (product no longer exists — telling the user to "check their inputs" is actively wrong), or a 5xx (server/infra failure — again nothing to do with the user's input). The 404 case is reachable in practice: a user who leaves a product detail page open while the catalog changes underneath them (or simply retries after some other failure) gets steered toward re-checking a form that was never the problem.

- **`submitSuccess()` has no time-based or interaction-based expiry beyond the next submit.** After a successful submission, "Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewertung!" is displayed and only cleared at the start of the *next* `submitRating()` call — not when the user starts editing the form again (`onAuthorNameChange`/`onScoreChange` don't touch it). A user who submits, then decides to also rate a second time with a different score, sees a stale "thank you" banner sitting above the form the entire time they're filling it in again, which reads as confirmation of nothing in particular.

- **`sprint-status.yaml` promotes the story straight to `review` despite `deferred-work.md` self-documenting an unresolved, direct AC 3 violation risk** (the case-insensitive-collation duplicate-author scenario, explicitly flagged as "jetzt aktiv statt rein theoretisch" — i.e., no longer just latent). - **No test exercises a non-uniform average** (e.g., three ratings that don't divide evenly, like 4+4+5 → 4.333...). All current test fixtures use rating sets that produce clean decimals (4.0, 5.0, 3.0), so nothing in the suite would catch a rounding/precision regression in either the backend's `double` arithmetic or the frontend's `.toFixed(1)` display path — arguably the most failure-prone numeric computation in the whole feature is the one never tested with an ugly number.

This may be an accepted simplification for a seed project, but it's not called out anywhere in the diff or in `deferred-work.md` as a conscious trade-off, so it reads as an oversight rather than a decision.

- **Aggregate computation (`AverageRating`/`RatingCount` from a full `Select(...).ToListAsync()` over `Score`) is duplicated verbatim between `RatingService.SubmitRatingAsync` and `CatalogService.GetProductDetailAsync`**, with no shared helper. Any future change (e.g., rounding rules, excluding flagged ratings) has two call sites to remember to update, and the diff didn't refactor the existing one when adding the second.

For a seed dataset this is invisible, but it's a pattern now established twice in the codebase, and it's exactly the kind of thing that becomes a real cost once rating volume grows.

- **The riskiest code path in the change — the `DbUpdateException` retry/fallback branch — has zero test coverage.** All four `RatingServiceTests` exercise only the straight-line paths (new rating, same-author replace, different authors, unknown product). Nothing simulates the concurrent-insert race the comment block explicitly describes and defends; the one piece of logic dense enough to need a comment explaining it is also the one piece nobody bothered to test.

- **Frontend collapses all HTTP failure modes into one generic message.** `submitRating()`'s `error` handler in `product-detail.ts:74-77` sets the same `'Bewertung konnte nicht gespeichert werden. Bitte Eingaben prüfen.'` regardless of whether the server returned 400 (bad input — message is appropriate), 404 (product no longer exists — telling the user to "check their inputs" is actively wrong), or a 5xx (server/infra failure — again nothing to do with the user's input). The 404 case is reachable in practice: a user who leaves a product detail page open while the catalog changes underneath them (or simply retries after some other failure) gets steered toward re-checking a form that was never the problem.

- **`submitSuccess()` has no time-based or interaction-based expiry beyond the next submit.** After a successful submission, "Vielen Dank für Ihre Bewertung!" is displayed and only cleared at the start of the *next* `submitRating()` call — not when the user starts editing the form again (`onAuthorNameChange`/`onScoreChange` don't touch it). A user who submits, then decides to also rate a second time with a different score, sees a stale "thank you" banner sitting above the form the entire time they're filling it in again, which reads as confirmation of nothing in particular.

- **`sprint-status.yaml` promotes the story straight to `review` despite `deferred-work.md` self-documenting an unresolved, direct AC 3 violation risk** (the case-insensitive-collation duplicate-author scenario, explicitly flagged as "jetzt aktiv statt rein theoretisch" — i.e., no longer just latent).
